I was talking with my son a few months ago about the anti-bullying campaign his school was doing. I was shocked that he hadn't known a single kid who was involved in a fist fight.

I went to school in the 70's and 80's. Typical teacher response to two kids getting in an argument back then was "take it outside". I had that feeling in the pit of my stomach when I knew that I would have to walk outside to face a group of bullys after school. I would love to say otherwise, but I lost far more fights then I won.

Still, it helped to define me as a person. I can't imagine how difficult confrontation would be if I grew up never experiencing fighting at school.

So what did you grow up with that kids today don't have?
What was it that defined your childhood that the current generation lacks?
Face-to-face interaction and needing to go outside for entertainment.

It's so strange to think of a generation that doesn't just walk over to their friend's house to play. I don't think my son has ever initiated a visit, and he's 14.

I have to practically kick him out of the house for him to go ride his bike.
It's a strange world; I honestly don't envy our kids' childhoods. Too much umbrella parenting and too few risks taken.

Being told to get outside to play and not to come home until tea-time. Like serious levels of freedom and (according to today's attitudes) child neglect. We'd spend all day wandering the woods and moors, getting into shit, swimming, climbing, etc. And I mean from the age of six or seven. Not one of my colleagues let their precious little darlings out of their sight.

So true, looking back at it now all our parents would be in jail nowadays. I recall my mum telling me off as a child for watching a show on how to build a raft, I was barely in the house for 5 minutes. I recall her saying don't watch that go and build it ! and also telling me go out make your knees green, fall out a tree just do something. I am not sure if she ever regretted saying that as the amount of shoes and clothes I went thought must of cost her a packet due to mucking it up outside. Then again it was cheap for a reason :)
This more than anything defined my childhood too.

Spending the entire summer outside, running around the general neighborhood areas. I was reading something recently about how parents don't really allow children to just be outside on their bikes. They keep them tethered very closely to home.

Freedom. We are the last generation of humans to know what life was like without electronic monitoring, dog leash cell phones, or cameras in the sky.

Children In 2050 will ask how we survived the terror and danger of being alone sometimes.

roaming around from a young age with other children from the neighborhood without parental supervision. parents that didn't focus all of their attention on the children at social gatherings, children were expected to play amongst themselves while the parents did adult things.
AM radio when you heard some of everything

It can be a messy topic, but I am somewhat partial to the views of Jürgen Habermas:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Habermas#Religious_dialogue

However, when discussing issues of public policy, I do think it is necessary for those who hold religious beliefs to put forth some amount of labor and effort in translating their beliefs into secular language, which can be understood by a wider audience.

That is, when engaged in public advocacy, for policy decisions affecting other people, it is not sufficient for a religious person to justify their position solely using biblical arguments. This is because such arguments tend to be exclusionary, and inaccessible to other members of society who are not members of that particular religion.

So, as long as the above criteria is met when engaged in discussions of policy, I personally do not mind religious discussion, and do not think that one should feel pressured into hiding their religious beliefs.
